concepts.maxim: Treat others as you would wish to be treated.
concepts.summary: Perhaps the most widely shared rule for living. Long before these traditions could read one another, each arrived at the same quiet test: before you act, put yourself in the other person's place.

concepts.maxim: Life contains suffering; begin by accepting it.
concepts.summary: Not a counsel of despair, but a starting point. Naming the hardness of life honestly frees us to respond to it with courage rather than surprise.

links.label: The Dhammapada, tr. F. Max Müller (free text, Sacred Texts)

concepts.maxim: Craving is the root of suffering.
concepts.summary: Much of our pain comes not from what happens, but from our grasping for things to be otherwise. Loosen the grip and the weight lightens.

links.label: The Dhammapada, tr. F. Max Müller (free text, Sacred Texts)

concepts.maxim: Be present: the here and now is where life happens.
concepts.summary: The past has gone and the future has not arrived. The present moment is the only place we can actually live, act and enjoy.

links.label: Eckhart Tolle, The Power of Now (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Treat yourself like someone you are responsible for helping.
concepts.summary: We often care better for others than for ourselves. Extend the same kindness and discipline inward.

links.label: Jordan B. Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Find meaning in the struggle itself.
concepts.summary: Sisyphus pushes his boulder up the hill forever. The ancient myth was a punishment; the modern reading asks whether the effort itself can be enough.

links.label: Ryan Holiday, The Obstacle Is the Way (Open Library)
Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (Open Library)
Joseph Campbell, The Hero with a Thousand Faces (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Leave things better than you found them.
concepts.summary: A simple measure for a day, a campsite or a life: did the world come out a little ahead for your having passed through?

concepts.maxim: Keep it simple.
concepts.summary: Complexity is costly and fragile. The simplest design that works is usually the one that lasts.

concepts.maxim: A few causes drive most results (the 80/20 rule).
concepts.summary: Effort and outcome are rarely in proportion. Find the vital few things that matter and give them your best attention.

links.label: Greg McKeown, Essentialism (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: People rise to their level of incompetence.
concepts.summary: A gently humbling observation about organisations: we tend to be promoted until we land in a role we no longer do well. Know your strengths.

links.label: Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull, The Peter Principle (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Happiness is reality minus expectations.
concepts.summary: A popular modern formula. When expectations outrun reality, disappointment fills the gap; holding them lightly leaves room for contentment.

links.label: Mark Manson, The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Do your work wholeheartedly and with skill.
concepts.summary: Whatever is in front of you, give it your full strength. Skill grows quietly out of repeated, careful effort, and in time it opens doors.

links.label: James Clear, Atomic Habits (Open Library)
Josh Waitzkin, The Art of Learning (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Pursue what is meaningful, not what is merely profitable.
concepts.summary: Chase the thing that matters to you rather than the quick reward. A life built around meaning tends to carry its own momentum.

links.label: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (Wikipedia)
Jordan B. Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Ability grows with effort; measure yourself against who you were yesterday.
concepts.summary: Talents are a starting point, not a verdict. The useful comparison is with your own past self, and every honest effort moves the line.

links.label: Carol S. Dweck, Mindset (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: More choice does not always mean more happiness.
concepts.summary: An endless menu can leave us anxious and second-guessing. Sometimes choosing 'good enough' and letting go is the wiser path.

links.label: Barry Schwartz, The Paradox of Choice (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: There is a time for everything; give your days a rhythm.
concepts.summary: Life moves in seasons and cycles. A steady rhythm of rising, working, eating and resting makes room for everything else.

links.label: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Tell the truth, or at least don't lie.
concepts.summary: Honesty keeps our footing sure. Each small truth makes the world, and ourselves, a little easier to trust.

concepts.maxim: Your thoughts shape your life.
concepts.summary: What we dwell on becomes the lens we see through, and then the ground we stand on. Tending the mind is tending the life.

links.label: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (Wikipedia)
The Dhammapada, tr. F. Max Müller (free text, Sacred Texts)

concepts.maxim: Seek the middle way; avoid extremes.
concepts.summary: Too much and too little both lead us astray. Again and again the old teachers point to a balanced path between the extremes, harder to find than either, but steadier to walk.

concepts.maxim: Meet hatred with love and evil with good.
concepts.summary: Answering harm with harm only keeps the wheel turning. Many traditions ask something harder and braver: to break the cycle by returning kindness, even to an enemy.

concepts.maxim: Know yourself.
concepts.summary: Understanding the world begins close to home. To look honestly at our own motives, limits and ignorance is a lifelong task, and perhaps the beginning of every other kind of wisdom.

concepts.maxim: Be humble; pride goes before a fall.
concepts.summary: Those who lift themselves up tend to be brought low, while those who hold themselves lightly are trusted and remembered. Humility is not thinking less of ourselves, but seeing ourselves truly.

links.label: Ryan Holiday, Ego Is the Enemy (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Be slow to anger; master yourself.
concepts.summary: Anger arrives quickly and leaves damage behind it. Real strength, these voices agree, lies less in overpowering others than in holding the reins of our own temper.

concepts.maxim: Remember that you will die, and live well today.
concepts.summary: Our days are numbered, and remembering it is not morbid but clarifying. Keeping death in view shrinks petty quarrels and turns us back towards what is good while we still can.

links.label: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (free text, Project Gutenberg)

concepts.maxim: Speak kindly, or keep silent.
concepts.summary: Words can heal or wound, and once spoken they cannot be taken back. A little restraint in speech spares others pain and spares us a good deal of trouble.

concepts.maxim: Give thanks.
concepts.summary: Gratitude turns what we have into enough, and it notices the kindness we would otherwise take for granted. Saying thank you, to people and to life, softens the heart and makes room for joy.

concepts.maxim: Forgive, and keep forgiving.
concepts.summary: Everyone stumbles, and everyone needs pardon at some point. Letting go of a grievance frees the one who forgives as much as the one forgiven.

concepts.maxim: Give freely; generosity enriches the giver.
concepts.summary: What we give away has a strange way of coming back as a fuller life. An open hand makes room for connection, and it loosens the grip that possessions can have on us.

links.label: Adam Grant, Give and Take (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Everything passes; hold things lightly.
concepts.summary: Nothing we see stays the same, not our troubles, our triumphs or the world around us. Remembering this can steady us in hard times and keep us gentle in good ones.

links.label: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (free text, Project Gutenberg)

concepts.maxim: Do what is right, even when you are afraid.
concepts.summary: Courage is not the absence of fear but the choice to act well in its presence. Most of the good we do asks a little bravery of us.

links.label: Brené Brown, Daring Greatly (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Be patient; endure, and let things ripen.
concepts.summary: Much of what matters grows slowly and cannot be hurried. Patience is the quiet strength that holds steady through difficulty and waits for the right moment.

concepts.maxim: Great things begin with small steps.
concepts.summary: Every large work starts as something tiny and easy to overlook. Taking the next small step, and being faithful in little things, is how anything worthwhile gets built.

links.label: BJ Fogg, Tiny Habits (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Look to your own faults before judging others.
concepts.summary: It is easy to see what others get wrong and hard to see our own failings. Turning the light on ourselves first makes us both wiser and kinder.

concepts.maxim: Choose your companions wisely.
concepts.summary: We slowly become like the people we spend our days with. Seeking out good, honest friends is one of the surest ways to grow into a better person.

concepts.maxim: Welcome the stranger.
concepts.summary: Almost every tradition treats the guest and the traveller as someone to honour. Opening our door, and our table, reminds us that we too have been strangers somewhere.

concepts.maxim: Honour your father and your mother.
concepts.summary: The people who raised us gave us our first world, however imperfectly. Many traditions ask us to meet them with care and respect, not just duty, and to let that gratitude show in how we treat them as they grow older.

concepts.maxim: Let your actions match your words.
concepts.summary: Fine words cost little; what we do shows what we really believe. Living out what we say, quietly and first, is how trust is built, in others and in ourselves.

concepts.maxim: Keep learning, all your life.
concepts.summary: Learning is not a stage we finish but a way of staying awake to the world. Traditions far apart describe it as a quiet pleasure, the mark of someone wise enough to know there is always more to hear.

concepts.maxim: Listen more than you speak.
concepts.summary: Real listening is a kind of generosity, and a kind of humility too. When we assume the other person may know something we don't, conversations stop being contests and start teaching us.

links.label: Stephen R. Covey, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Do what is just, even when it costs you.
concepts.summary: Justice asks us to be fair when fairness is inconvenient: to our rivals, to strangers, and against our own interest. Many traditions hold that it is better to suffer a wrong than to do one, and that a fair heart is worth more than any advantage.

concepts.maxim: Be merciful to every living being.
concepts.summary: Mercy is kindness offered where it was not earned. Traditions across the world ask us to widen our care, from family to stranger to every creature that breathes, and find that a softer heart is also a freer one.

concepts.maxim: Seek peace, and pursue it.
concepts.summary: Peace rarely arrives by itself; it is something we go after, in quarrels at home as much as between nations. To be the one who lowers the temperature, and who takes the offered hand, is honoured in nearly every tradition.

concepts.maxim: First, do no harm.
concepts.summary: Before we try to help, we can at least refuse to hurt. This simple restraint, shared by healers, monks and moralists, asks us to remember that every living being, like us, fears pain and loves life.

concepts.maxim: Keep your promises; let your yes mean yes.
concepts.summary: A promise is a small piece of the future we give to someone else. Keeping it, or not making it lightly, is how trust grows, and how our words come to carry weight.

concepts.maxim: Make time for stillness.
concepts.summary: Much of our restlessness comes from never stopping. Contemplatives, philosophers and psalmists alike point to a quiet place within, always available, where we can rest, see clearly and return refreshed.

concepts.maxim: Admit your mistakes and put them right.
concepts.summary: Everyone falls short; what matters is what we do next. Owning a fault, rather than hiding it, is the first step to mending it, and a mended fault can leave us brighter than before.

links.label: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin, Extreme Ownership (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: When you fall, get back up.
concepts.summary: Falling is not the failure; staying down is. Traditions far apart in time and place honour the person who stumbles, gathers themselves, and rises again, as many times as it takes.

concepts.maxim: Advantage tends to compound: those who have, get more.
concepts.summary: Early advantages (a head start, a good name, a little capital) tend to attract more of the same, while those with little often find even that slipping away. The Gospel of Matthew states the pattern twice, and in 1968 the sociologists Robert K. Merton and Harriet Zuckerman named it the Matthew effect. Seeing it clearly invites us to share a head start generously and to lift up those who begin behind.

links.label: Malcolm Gladwell, Outliers (Open Library)

concepts.maxim: Be kind to animals.
concepts.summary: Animals feel hunger, fear and pain, and many of them live in our care or at our mercy. Traditions far apart treat the way we treat them as a quiet measure of our character, and kindness to a thirsty creature as a good deed in its own right.

concepts.maxim: Rise to your work.
concepts.summary: On the mornings when we would rather stay in bed, the work in front of us is still ours to do. Many traditions treat idleness as a slow loss and honest effort as part of what it means to live fully.

concepts.maxim: You reap what you sow.
concepts.summary: What we do does not simply vanish; it comes back to shape our own lives. Traditions across the world picture our deeds returning to us, as surely as a harvest follows the seed or a shadow follows its body.

concepts.maxim: Give full measure: deal honestly in trade.
concepts.summary: Fair weights and honest measures are among the oldest moral rules we know. Cheating in small ways, a short measure here or a fake mixed in with the genuine there, wears away the trust that every exchange depends on.

quotes.translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis)

quotes.text: 'Tis never good to let the thought of good things done thee pass away; / Of things not good, 'tis good to rid thy memory that very day.
quotes.work: Tirukkural, kural 108, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /
quotes.translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis)

quotes.text: When pleasant words are easy, bitter words to use, / Is, leaving sweet ripe fruit, the sour unripe to choose.
quotes.work: Tirukkural, kural 100, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /
quotes.translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis)

quotes.text: In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below; / The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow.
quotes.work: Tirukkural, kural 396, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /
quotes.translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis)

quotes.text: The sons of Adam are members one of another, for in their creation they have a common origin. If the vicissitudes of fortune involve one member in pain, all the other members will feel a sympathy. Thou, who art indifferent to other men's affliction, if they call thee a man art unworthy of the name.
quotes.work: Gulistan, ch. I, story X, tr. James Ross (1823), in Persian Literature, vol. 2 (Colonial Press, 1900); verse rendered as prose by the translator

quotes.text: patience is bitter, yet it will yield sweet fruit.
quotes.work: Gulistan, ch. I, story XVI, tr. James Ross (1823), in Persian Literature, vol. 2 (Colonial Press, 1900)

quotes.text: A learned man without works is a bee without honey
quotes.work: Gulistan, ch. VIII, maxim LXXXVI, tr. James Ross (1823), in Persian Literature, vol. 2 (Colonial Press, 1900)

quotes.text: How couldst thou forget thine own faults and busy thyself with the faults of others? Whoso doeth this is accursed of Me.
quotes.work: The Hidden Words, Arabic no. 26, tr. Shoghi Effendi

quotes.text: Bring thyself to account each day ere thou art summoned to a reckoning; for death, unheralded, shall come upon thee and thou shalt be called to give account for thy deeds.
quotes.work: The Hidden Words, Arabic no. 31, tr. Shoghi Effendi

quotes.text: Break not the contract, O Spitama! neither the one that thou hadst entered into with one of the unfaithful, nor the one that thou hadst entered into with one of the faithful who is one of thy own faith. For Mithra stands for both the faithful and the unfaithful.
quotes.work: Avesta, Mihr Yasht (Yasht 10) 2, tr. James Darmesteter (Sacred Books of the East 23, 1883); footnote numbers removed

quotes.text: He who forgives ends the quarrel.
quotes.work: Yoruba proverb 24, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: Not to aid one in distress is to kill him in your heart.
quotes.work: Yoruba proverb 71, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: Continual sweepings make a dust-heap.
quotes.work: Yoruba proverb 6, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: If one is carrying water, and it gets spilt, so long as the calabash is not broken one can still get more.
quotes.work: Yoruba proverb 146, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: Anger does nobody good, / But patience is the father of kindness. / Anger draws arrows from the quiver, / But good words draw kola-nuts from the bag.
quotes.work: Yoruba aphorism 5 (couplet sayings), as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII; line breaks shown as /. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: One falsehood spoils a thousand truths.
quotes.work: Ashanti Proverbs, no. 609, tr. R. Sutherland Rattray (Oxford, 1916), from J. G. Christaller's Twi collection (1879). The saying is older than its recording.

quotes.text: It is to regard the state of others as one's own, the houses of others as one's own, the persons of others as one's self.
quotes.work: Mozi, Book 4, Universal Love II, tr. W. P. Mei (1929). Wording checked via the page text shown in a web search index; the page itself blocks automated fetching, so not checked directly.
quotes.translation: translation (W. P. Mei), as published on ctext.org

quotes.text: He ought to pity the malignant tendencies of others; to rejoice over their excellences; to help them in their straits; to rescue them from their perils; to regard their gains as if they were his own, and their losses in the same way
quotes.thinker: Treatise of the Most Exalted One on Action and Response
quotes.work: The Thai-Shang Tractate of Actions and Their Retributions (Taishang Ganying Pian), 3, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 40, 1891)

quotes.text: There is now a change again, and she is dead. The relation between these things is like the procession of the four seasons from spring to autumn, from winter to summer.
quotes.work: Zhuangzi, Book XVIII (Perfect Enjoyment), 2, on the death of his wife, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 40, 1891)

quotes.text: Let us cease from wrath, and refrain from angry looks. Nor let us be resentful when others differ from us. For all men have hearts, and each heart has its own leanings.
quotes.work: Seventeen-Article Constitution (604), art. X, in Nihongi, Book XXII, tr. W. G. Aston (1896)

quotes.text: Harmony is to be valued, and an avoidance of wanton opposition to be honoured.
quotes.work: Seventeen-Article Constitution (604), art. I, in Nihongi, Book XXII, tr. W. G. Aston (1896); footnote marker removed

quotes.text: A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
quotes.work: Proverbs 12:10 (KJV)

quotes.text: A man is not an elect (Ariya) because he injures living creatures; because he has pity on all living creatures, therefore is a man called Ariya.
quotes.work: Dhammapada 270, tr. F. Max Müller

quotes.text: "Is there a reward for us in serving (the) animals?" He replied, "Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate."
quotes.work: Sahih al-Bukhari 2363 (narrated by Abu Huraira), the Prophet's answer after telling of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog
quotes.translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com

quotes.text: Knowing them, a wise man should not act sinfully towards animals, nor cause others to act so, nor allow others to act so.
quotes.work: Acaranga Sutra, Book I, Lecture 1, Lesson 6, tr. Hermann Jacobi (Sacred Books of the East 22)

quotes.work: Dhammapada 280, tr. F. Max Müller

quotes.work: Proverbs 6:6 (KJV)

quotes.work: Proverbs 22:8 (KJV)

quotes.text: according as he acts and according as he behaves, so will he be:--a man of good acts will become good, a man of bad acts, bad. He becomes pure by pure deeds, bad by bad deeds.
quotes.work: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad IV.4.5, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884)

quotes.text: Ashes fly back in the face of him who throws them.
quotes.work: Yoruba proverb 81, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII; Ellis glosses it as our "Curses come home to roost". The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: There are no special doors for calamity and happiness (in men's lot); they come as men themselves call them. Their recompenses follow good and evil as the shadow follows the substance.

quotes.work: Taittiriya Upanishad I.11.2, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884); the same charge honours mother, father and guest

quotes.text: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.
quotes.work: Leviticus 19:32 (KJV)

quotes.text: When there are no elders the town is ruined, / And when the master dies the house is desolate.
quotes.work: Yoruba aphorism 9 (couplet sayings), as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII; line breaks shown as /. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.

quotes.text: beware of the quality of covetousness, which is a grievous inner (?) malady. Let it not chance that thou fall thereinto. It setteth at variance fathers-in-law and the kinsmen of the daughter-in-law; it sundereth the wife and the husband. It gathereth unto itself all evils; it is the girdle of all wickedness.
quotes.work: The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §19, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906); the "(?)" is the translator's
